name: Narrative therapy
heroTitle: You are more than the story a problem tells about you.
summary: Narrative therapy explores identity, meaning, and the influence of problems. Learn how separating a person from a problem can make room for agency without denying facts or responsibility.
panelTitle: A description can become too small for a life.
panelParagraphs: I struggled in that conversation is different from I am a failure. Narrative work explores which descriptions dominate and what they leave out.

model.title: Separate the person from the problem, without denying its effects.
paragraphs: Narrative therapy is interested in the stories through which people make sense of experience. A problem can become so dominant in that story that it seems to define the whole person. Externalizing language separates identity from the difficulty so its effects can be examined more clearly.

This is not pretending a problem is imaginary or that actions have no consequences. A person can take responsibility for a harmful choice without reducing their entire identity to that choice. The work asks about influence, context, values, and responses rather than accepting a totalizing label.

Narrative conversations also consider cultural and social messages. Expectations about success, gender, family, ability, or belonging may shape the meanings a person has available. The therapist is not the authority who writes a better identity for you; preferred meanings should be grounded in your own experience.

panel.title: More than a positive reframe.
paragraphs: A preferred story needs detail and evidence from your life. Replacing a harsh label with a flattering slogan is not the same as discovering a richer account.

example.title: One difficult presentation becomes a story about being incapable.
example.intro: A fictional example about a problem-saturated description.

items.title: The dominant account
paragraphs: After stumbling during a presentation, Casey concludes that they are bad at anything requiring confidence. They begin declining opportunities to speak.

items.title: The problem's influence
paragraphs: The conversation explores how that conclusion affects choices, attention, and relationships. It also asks what standards of success Casey is measuring themselves against.

items.title: Details left out
paragraphs: Casey remembers helping a new colleague understand a complex task. That moment does not erase the difficult presentation, but it complicates the claim that they cannot communicate.

reveal.title: What does a richer account make possible?
paragraphs: A narrative therapist might ask what Casey's helpful conversation says about care, preparation, or knowledge and who else has noticed those qualities. The aim is not to argue that the presentation was secretly excellent. It is to keep one event from controlling the entire description of Casey's abilities.

A different story may support different choices, but those choices still need real-world practice and support. This example is fictional and does not establish a cause or treatment plan for someone else's anxiety.

toolsTitle: Ways the conversation can make room for another account.
toolsIntro: The language should fit the person. Naming a problem is an invitation, not a required exercise.

tools.title: Externalizing the problem
tools.teaser: Explore what a difficulty does rather than equating it with who you are.
paragraphs: A therapist may use language such as the influence of worry rather than calling a person a worrier. The next questions concern when that influence grows, what it asks of the person, and how they respond.
Externalizing is not a way to excuse behavior by blaming an invented entity. Accountability remains with the person making choices.

tools.title: Mapping influence
tools.teaser: Look at the relationship between the problem and daily life.
paragraphs: The work may examine how a problem affects work, relationships, decisions, and self-understanding, and how the person has responded to it. That two-way inquiry can reveal forms of agency that a single label overlooks.
Context matters: resisting a problem can be much harder without safety, resources, or support.

tools.title: Finding overlooked moments
tools.teaser: Notice experiences that do not fit the dominant story.
paragraphs: An exception or unique outcome is a moment that challenges a problem's claim to define everything. Its meaning is explored in detail: what happened, why it mattered, and which values or relationships were involved.
A moment does not have to be dramatic to be worth understanding. It also does not cancel the suffering that continues.

tools.title: Developing a preferred account
tools.teaser: Connect experiences, values, and future possibilities.
paragraphs: Conversations may link overlooked moments into a fuller description of identity and intention. Some therapists use letters or other reflective practices, with consent, to support that process.
The goal is an account the person recognizes as meaningful and credible, not a therapist-authored story they are expected to accept.

processTitle: A conversation about meaning can stay connected to action.

process.title: Name the concern in your language
paragraphs: Begin with the words you use and how the difficulty affects life. The therapist should not replace your account with a preferred theory before understanding it.

process.title: Explore the dominant story
paragraphs: Consider how the story developed, what reinforces it, and which contexts or social expectations give it authority.

process.title: Look for fuller details
paragraphs: Explore moments, relationships, values, and responses that are missing from the narrow account.

process.title: Consider what follows
paragraphs: A richer account may open a practical choice, a conversation, or a different way to seek support. Review whether it helps outside the session.

limitsTitle: Changing a story does not change every circumstance.

limits.title: Facts and responsibility remain
paragraphs: Narrative work is not rewriting history, denying an injury, or inventing evidence. It concerns how experience is interpreted and organized while preserving the reality of events and their consequences.

limits.title: Language should not become another demand
paragraphs: Some people prefer concrete skills, medical assessment, or another therapeutic style. A narrative perspective can be discussed as one part of a plan rather than imposed as the only meaningful way to work.

questions.question: Is this the same as telling my life story?
paragraphs: You may discuss life experiences, but the method is not just recounting a biography. It examines how meanings are formed, which stories dominate, and what other experiences and values deserve attention.

questions.question: Does externalizing mean the problem is not my responsibility?
paragraphs: No. Separating identity from a problem can reduce a totalizing judgment while leaving responsibility for behavior intact. A person can work to repair harm without being described as nothing but the harm.

questions.question: Do I need to enjoy writing?
paragraphs: No. Narrative therapy can take place through conversation. Writing or other reflective practices should be optional, purposeful, and adapted to you rather than treated as prerequisites.

questions.question: Can we discuss discrimination or social expectations?
paragraphs: Yes. Narrative therapy explicitly attends to cultural and social context. A problem should not be framed solely as an individual's story when real exclusion, inequity, or danger is involved.

questions.question: How would I know whether it is useful?
paragraphs: Consider whether the conversations produce a more accurate, less restrictive understanding and support meaningful choices. Feeling briefly encouraged is not the only measure; daily functioning and your own goals matter too.
